procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of the Central Road Traffic Board, approved by the Government in revision, which set aside the Regional Transport Authority's grant of a stage carriage permit to the appellant.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant moved the Allahabad High Court for a writ of certiorari to quash the proceedings of the Central Road Traffic Board and the Government. During the pendency of these proceedings, a stay order was in place, allowing the appellant to continue running his buses.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant approached the Supreme Court by special leave from the Judgment and order dated October 18, 1955, of the Allahabad High Court in Government Appeal No. 60•of 1953 arising out of the judgment and order dated July 8, 1952, of the Court of Sessions Judge at Bareilly in Criminal. Sessions Trial No. 27 of 1952.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the trial court's judgment of acquittal.

facts: The trial court (Sessions Judge) acquitted the appellant.
The State appealed this acquittal to the High Court.
The High Court reversed the trial court's decision, convicting the appellant.
The High Court found the trial judge's view to be "wholly erroneous" and one that "no reasonable person could have taken," which resulted in a "gross miscarriage of justice."
The High Court accepted the eyewitness testimony against the appellant, even while concluding that the same witnesses had falsely implicated another person, Qudrat Ullah.
law: The Supreme Court operates on the principle that a judgment of acquittal should not be reversed lightly. However, it can be overturned if the trial court's view is found to be completely erroneous and has resulted in a miscarriage of justice.
application: Recognizing that this was a case involving the reversal of an acquittal, the Supreme Court allowed the appellant's counsel to fully re-examine the evidence, including discrepancies in witness statements and other improbabilities.
The Supreme Court then conducted its own independent "review of the evidence of the prosecution witnesses."
After its review, the Supreme Court was "satisfied that the learned Judges [of the High Court] were justified in coming to the conclusion they did."
The Court explicitly agreed that "the view of the trial judge was rightly displaced."
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that upon its own review of the evidence, the appellant was rightly convicted. It therefore dismissed the appeal and affirmed the High Court's judgment, holding that the High Court was justified in reversing the trial court's acquittal.

issue.issue_text: Whether the conviction was sustainable despite alleged discrepancies in witness statements and improbabilities in the case.

facts: The appellant's counsel argued against the conviction by pointing out discrepancies in the statements of witnesses and improbabilities in the case.
The case involved a reversal of an acquittal by the trial court; the High Court had convicted the appellant.
The High Court had acknowledged that the eyewitnesses had falsely implicated another person (Qudrat Ullah) but still found their testimony credible regarding the appellant's guilt.
The High Court concluded that the trial judge's view was one "which no reasonable person could have taken" and that there was "not the slightest doubt" about the appellant's guilt.
law: The court is not bound by a rigid rule that a witness who is disbelieved on one part of their testimony must be rejected in their entirety. This is merely a "rule of caution."
It is the court's duty to review the evidence, including its discrepancies and improbabilities, to determine if the prosecution has proven its case.
application: The Supreme Court allowed the appellant's counsel to present a full analysis of the evidence, including the alleged discrepancies and improbabilities.
After conducting its own review of the evidence from the prosecution witnesses, the Supreme Court agreed with the High Court's assessment.

The Court found that the High Court was justified in sifting through the evidence, rejecting the improbable parts (regarding Qudrat Ullah) while accepting the credible parts that established the appellant's guilt.
The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court had rightly displaced the trial judge's erroneous view of the evidence.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the conviction was sustainable. After reviewing the evidence, it concluded that the High Court was justified in finding the appellant guilty, despite the noted discrepancies and the fact that witnesses had been untruthful about another aspect of the case. The appeal was therefore dismissed.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court adopted a wrong approach by making observations that came close to placing the burden of proof on the accused.

facts: The Supreme Court identified a specific passage in the High Court's judgment that it found problematic.

The High Court had observed: "The respondent himself did not have the courage to say that he did not find them at the spot. If he were innocent, he must have come out of his house immediately on hearing the noise and must have known who was present there and who was not."
law: The Supreme Court reiterated the "cardinal principle of criminal jurisprudence" which is the presumption of innocence of an accused person until proven guilty.
It is the duty of the prosecution to prove the prisoner's guilt, and the onus is not on the accused.
application: The Supreme Court found the High Court's observation to be "disconsolate and indicative of a wrong approach."

It held that the passage was "so destructive of the cardinal principle" because it speculated on what an innocent person "must have" done and criticized the accused for his silence or lack of a specific denial.

This line of reasoning, according to the Supreme Court, "comes perilously near to putting the burden on the accused if it does not actually do so," as it implies the accused had a duty to act or speak in a certain way to prove his innocence.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted that the High Court had adopted a wrong approach. It concluded that the High Court's observation improperly shifted the burden of proof onto the accused, which is contrary to the fundamental principle that an accused is presumed innocent and the prosecution must prove guilt.

issue.issue_text: Whether a particular doctrine should be elevated from a 'rule of caution' to a binding principle of law.

facts: An appellant argued that the testimony of certain witnesses should have been completely rejected.
The basis for this argument was that the witnesses had falsely implicated another accused person (Qudrat Ullah), and the lower courts had disbelieved that part of their testimony.
The appellant invoked the maxim 'falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus' (false in one thing, false in everything) to support this claim.
law: The Supreme Court stated that the maxim 'falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus' has not been generally accepted in India and has not achieved the status of a rule of law.
The Court defined the doctrine as merely a 'rule of caution,' not a 'mandatory rule of evidence.'
The Court also noted that legal authorities have described the maxim as 'worthless,' 'absolutely false as a maxim of life,' and 'in practice pernicious.'
application: The Court explained that as a 'rule of caution,' the maxim means that if a witness is found to be untruthful on one point, their testimony *may* be disregarded, but it does not mean it *must* be disregarded.
The decision to accept or reject the remainder of the testimony is a matter of weighing the evidence, which a court can do in the specific circumstances of a case.
By refusing to treat the maxim as a binding rule, the Court affirmed that a judge can believe part of a witness's testimony while disbelieving another part.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's attempt to elevate the doctrine from a 'rule of caution' to a binding principle of law, holding that it is not a mandatory rule in India and a court is not required to reject a witness's entire testimony just because a part of it is found to be false.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the trial court's judgment of acquittal.
appellant_arguments: The High Court was not justified in reversing the trial court's judgment of acquittal.
respondent_arguments: The reversal was justified because the trial judge's view was one 'which no reasonable person could have taken' and was a 'wholly erroneous view of the evidence which has resulted in gross miscarriage of justice'.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the conviction was sustainable despite alleged discrepancies in witness statements and improbabilities in the case.
appellant_arguments: The conviction is not sustainable due to discrepancies in the statements of witnesses and the improbabilities of the case.
respondent_arguments: The conviction is sustainable because the direct evidence from eyewitnesses made out a clear case against the appellant, and there was 'no sound reason for disregarding it'.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court adopted a wrong approach by making observations that came close to placing the burden of proof on the accused.
appellant_arguments: The High Court adopted a wrong approach with an observation that 'comes perilously near to putting the burden on the accused if it does not actually do so'.
respondent_arguments: The High Court's observation that the defendant's evidence was of 'no use to him' because the witnesses had given false evidence elsewhere was a valid assessment of witness credibility, not a shifting of the burden of proof.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a particular doctrine should be elevated from a 'rule of caution' to a binding principle of law.
appellant_arguments: Citing a Privy Council judgment, the appellant argued that a doctrine (likely 'falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus') should be treated as a binding principle of law, not merely a 'rule of caution'.
respondent_arguments: The doctrine should remain a 'rule of caution' and not be elevated to a binding legal principle.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The maxim 'falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus' is not a rule of law but merely a rule of caution; it is not a mandatory rule of evidence that testimony must be disregarded, but rather a matter of the weight of evidence that a court may apply.
obiter: It is the duty of the prosecution to prove the prisoner's guilt, subject to any statutory exception.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Upon a review of the evidence of the prosecution witnesses, the Court concluded that the appellant was rightly convicted. The High Court was justified in reversing the trial court's judgment of acquittal because the trial judge's view was one 'which no reasonable person could have taken' and was a 'wholly erroneous view of the evidence which has resulted in gross miscarriage of justice'. Despite a flawed observation by the High Court regarding the burden of proof, the direct evidence from eyewitnesses made out a clear case against the appellant.
legal_tests_applied: The standard for reversing a judgment of acquittal is whether the trial judge's view was one 'which no reasonable person could have taken' and was a 'wholly erroneous view of the evidence which has resulted in gross miscarriage of justice'.

The maxim 'falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus' is not a rule of law but 'merely a rule of caution.' It means that the testimony of a witness who has lied on one point 'may be disregarded and not that it must be disregarded.' It is not a 'mandatory rule of evidence'.

The cardinal principle of criminal jurisprudence is the 'presumed innocence of an accused person till otherwise proved,' and 'it is the duty of the prosecution to prove the prisoner's guilt ..... . subject to any statutory exception.'
why_appellant_lost: The Court, upon its own review of the evidence, was satisfied that the High Court was justified in reversing the acquittal and that the appellant was rightly convicted based on the direct evidence.

The appellant's argument that the entire testimony of eyewitnesses should be rejected because they falsely implicated another person (Qudrat Ullah) was dismissed. The Court refused to elevate the maxim 'falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus' to a binding rule of law, holding it is merely a rule of caution.

The Court rejected the appellant's argument that a Privy Council judgment conferred on the 'falsus in uno' doctrine the status of anything 'higher than a rule of caution,' noting the doctrine has been termed 'worthless' and 'pernicious' by authorities on evidence law.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's position that the reversal of acquittal was justified was accepted, as the Court affirmed the High Court's finding that the trial judge's view was wholly erroneous and resulted in a gross miscarriage of justice.

The respondent's argument that the conviction was sustainable based on direct evidence was upheld. The Court agreed with the High Court that 'The direct evidence made out a clear case against him and there was no sound reason for disregarding it.'
The respondent's position that the 'falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus' maxim is merely a rule of caution and not a binding principle of law was affirmed by the Court.
policy_considerations: The Court found it necessary to reiterate the cardinal principle of the presumed innocence of an accused, criticizing a passage in the High Court's judgment as 'so destructive' of this principle. The High Court's observation that the defendant's evidence was of 'no use to him' because his witnesses had given false evidence elsewhere was deemed to 'come perilously near to putting the burden on the accused if it does not actually do so.'
